chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
title: Jelly Roll Morton on the corner and his boogie-woogie story
summary: Jackson listened to Jelly Roll Morton telling stories at 132nd and Seventh and recalls his claim that boogie-woogie was New Orleans race horse music.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band

blocks.x: Did you know Jelly Roll Morton at all?
Yes, I knew Jelly Roll. I used to listen at him standing on the corner of 132nd and Seventh Avenue and he told a lot of stories.

One of the great stories that he told that I remember was when he used to play piano in a house of ill repute in New Orleans and he said he'd laugh at these guys today because they called it boogie-woogie piano, but down there during racing season the race horse players would come by the house of ill repute. And the minute they come by
they used to go into the boogie-woogie thing, da-ta da-ta da-ta da-ta. He said they called that race horse music 'cause it sounded like the horses galloping.
But he said they got the nerve to call it boogie-woogie, you know.
Yeah, he was a strong guy, wasn't he?
Oh, he was strong. He could tell you some stories, and I used to stand up in the corner, and, of course, there's a lot of things I can't say, you know.
But you would stand there all day listening to him alone.
Yeah, he could really sell himself. I just want to say I'm starting this tape 2 here --
-- on Quentin Jackson on this Sunday January 14 13th, 19- -- this Sunday, April, 10, 1976.
I'm talking to Quentin Jackson. I keep referring to him as Butter which is his nickname which was given to him during the Don Redmon days because of his blond complexion and his sort of portliness.
We were talking about Jelly Roll Morton.
